items.prompt: Define the production possibility curve (PPC).
items.canonical_answer: A production possibility curve is a boundary showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce in a given period when its resources are employed fully and efficiently.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must give the precise meaning of the term, and each creditable element of it is worth one mark.

items.prompt: An economy produces two goods: canned fish processed at Walvis Bay and maize meal milled at Otavi. Its planners decide to shift workers and tins from the mills into the canneries. Discuss how a production possibility curve for this economy is drawn and then used to show the change: set out what each axis is labelled with, where the original curve sits, the direction of the move along it, the point the economy ends at, and what the finished diagram shows in words.
items.canonical_answer: Label the vertical axis maize meal and the horizontal axis canned fish, both in tonnes per year. Draw PPC1 bowed outward from 60 000 tonnes of maize meal (no fish) to 30 000 tonnes of fish (no maize meal). Mark A on it at 40 000 tonnes of maize meal with 20 000 tonnes of fish. Moving workers and tins into the canneries is a movement along the curve: slide down PPC1 toward the fish axis to B, 25 000 tonnes of maize meal with 25 000 tonnes of fish, and label B as the new combination. In words: fish rose by 25 000 - 20 000 = 5 000 tonnes and maize meal fell by 40 000 - 25 000 = 15 000 tonnes, so 15 000 tonnes of maize meal is the opportunity cost of the extra fish. The curve has not moved: capacity is unchanged and only the choice has changed.
marking_guidance: Axes labelled: each axis named with its good and its unit; the two goods are the measures here, and money or price axes belong to other diagrams and earn nothing.
Original curves drawn and labelled: the single boundary drawn bowed outward between the intercepts and labelled PPC1 before any change is marked.
The shift or movement, in the correct direction: here a movement along the curve from A down the boundary toward the fish axis, since capacity is unchanged.
New point marked and labelled: the finishing combination B marked and named on the same curve.
What the diagram shows, in words: the reallocation from maize meal to fish, with the opportunity cost stated in tonnes.
The link: the definition supplies the boundary, and the consequence is the sacrificed maize measured on it.

items.prompt: A class in Windhoek lists what their two-good economy could produce in a year, at full and efficient use: P, no fish and 60 tonnes of maize; Q, 10 tonnes of fish and 55 tonnes of maize; R, 20 tonnes of fish and 45 tonnes of maize; S, 30 tonnes of fish and 30 tonnes of maize; T, 40 tonnes of fish and no maize. Explain what the data shows about the relationship between the two outputs.
items.canonical_answer: The data show a negative relationship: as fish rises from 0 to 40 tonnes, maize falls from 60 to 0. Comparing steps, P to Q costs 5 tonnes of maize for 10 tonnes of fish, but S to T costs 30 tonnes for the same 10, so the sacrifice grows. This is because the same workers and boats cannot be in both industries, and the resources best suited to fishing are moved first. However, these are maximums at full use; idle boats would leave output below them.
marking_guidance: What the data shows: the relationship between the two outputs must be stated before anything else.
Supporting evidence: a comparison of two rows or steps in the data, with their figures.
Exception: an answer that notes where the reading does not go further (boundary maximums, unrecorded output, a point inside rather than on the curve) earns the however mark.
Why: the explanation of the relationship - scarce resources shared between the two goods, with the resources best suited to the expanding good moved first and the least suited last.

items.prompt: Etosha Gate Lodge has 18 staff on fixed shifts and splits them between guided drives and the laundry. With every member guiding it runs 90 drives a month; with every member in laundry it turns around 360 laundry loads a month; mixed teams give the combinations between. Using the figures, explain why the lodge's month is a production possibility curve in miniature and what the boundary means for the lodge.
items.canonical_answer: The same 18 staff can run 90 guided drives a month or turn around 360 laundry loads, with mixed teams giving the combinations between: these are the two ends of a boundary. Because the staff are finite, every extra drive means laundry waiting, so the two outputs trade off. That is a PPC at firm level: the maximum combinations of two outputs from fixed resources. Therefore the boundary tells the manager what extra drives cost in laundry loads, and a month inside it means staff were idle.
marking_guidance: Context: the figures in the prompt must be used - no answer without them.
Reasoning: the link from the figures to the concept must be written out, because figures stated without the link earn nothing.
Conclusion: therefore the answer ends by saying what the figures show about the boundary.

items.prompt: Oshakati Textiles employs 40 machinists on two lines, school shirts and work dresses. A flu season leaves 6 of the 40 off work for a month while the factory keeps its order book open. Analyse the consequences for the firm's position relative to its production possibility boundary, and for its customers and its workers.
items.canonical_answer: With 6 of the 40 machinists off sick, fewer hands run the same machines, so output of both school shirts and work dresses falls. The factory therefore moves from a point on its boundary to a point inside it, because the boundary is drawn for all 40 at work. The boundary itself has not moved: the shortfall is in the use of resources, not in capacity. Customers wait longer for both lines, the 34 machinists at work face overtime pressure, and the firm's revenue for the month falls with its output.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change must be stated, as a when or an if.
Mechanism: the causal link must be written out, because this causes that, step by step.
Consequence: therefore the results are traced to output, employment or capacity.
For whom: each consequence is named for the consumer, the worker, the firm or the economy it lands on.

items.prompt: A study card lists what a set-out PPC must contain. Explain the features a learner should name when drawing a production possibility curve for an economy.
items.canonical_answer: First, each axis is labelled with one of the two goods and its unit per period, because the curve is drawn in goods, not money. Second, the curve slopes downward: at full use, more of one good means less of the other. Third, it tends to bow outward, because resources are not equally suited to both goods, so the sacrifice grows along it. Fourth, points mark combinations: a point on the curve is a maximum, and a point's position against the curve carries its meaning.
marking_guidance: Features: the elements required are named in the answer, and one mark is earned per feature developed with what it shows.

items.prompt: A news headline says an economy "is producing inside its PPC". Define what is meant by a point under, a point on and a point beyond a PPC.
items.canonical_answer: A point under the PPC shows resources idle or misused, so output could be higher. A point on it shows resources fully and efficiently employed. A point beyond it shows output that current resources and technology cannot produce.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must give the precise meaning of the term, and each creditable element of it is worth one mark.

items.prompt: An island economy farms rice and catches shrimp, and wants a picture that separates the combinations it can reach from those it cannot, with 14% of its boats idle this season. Discuss how a production possibility curve is drawn for the island and used to place three points - one at full use, one with the idle boats, and one the island hopes for but cannot yet reach: state the axes, the original curve, where each point sits relative to it, the point the island lands at once its boats work, and what the diagram shows in words.
items.canonical_answer: Label the vertical axis rice and the horizontal axis shrimp, both in tonnes per season. Draw PPC1 bowed outward between the two intercepts and label it. Mark Y on the curve at 50 tonnes of rice with 20 tonnes of shrimp: full and efficient use. Mark X inside it at 40 tonnes of rice with 14 tonnes of shrimp, below Y on both goods: this is where the island stands with 14% of its boats idle. Mark Z beyond it at 60 tonnes of rice with 25 tonnes of shrimp: out of reach with current resources. When the boats return to work, the island moves from X toward the curve, not along it, and its new point is on PPC1 at or near Y. In words: the curve separates what the island can reach from what it cannot, and from inside it both goods can rise together without sacrifice.
marking_guidance: Axes labelled: each axis named with its good and its unit; rice on one axis, shrimp on the other.
Original curves drawn and labelled: the single boundary drawn bowed outward and labelled PPC1 before the points are marked.

The shift or movement, in the correct direction: here no slide along the boundary occurs - the economy moves from inside toward the boundary, which is a change of location, not a movement along the curve.
New point marked and labelled: the point reached on the boundary once the idle boats are back at work.
What the diagram shows, in words: the boundary separating reachable from unreachable combinations, and the interior point showing unused boats.
The link: the boundary tells where a point may sit, and the consequence of idle boats is the interior location.

items.prompt: An island economy records two boundary combinations it could reach at full and efficient use: K, 12 000 tonnes of rice and 6 000 tonnes of shrimp, and L, 5 000 tonnes of rice and 11 000 tonnes of shrimp. Last season it actually produced 10 000 tonnes of rice and 5 000 tonnes of shrimp. Explain what the data shows about where the economy produced, and why.
items.canonical_answer: The data show the economy produced inside its boundary. At K it could have had 12 000 tonnes of rice and 6 000 tonnes of shrimp; last season's 10 000 and 5 000 tonnes are below K on both goods. So some resources were idle or misused, and both goods could have risen without sacrifice. However, part of the gap may be unrecorded output, such as rice kept for home use, so the true point may lie closer to the boundary.

items.prompt: A Katima Mulilo co-operative with 12 members could make up to 60 reed mats or 30 fish baskets a month at full stretch, with the combinations between, including 40 reed mats together with 22 fish baskets. In March it recorded 40 reed mats and 12 fish baskets. Using the figures, explain where March sits relative to the co-operative's boundary and what that location shows.
items.canonical_answer: The boundary includes 40 reed mats with 22 fish baskets a month. March produced the same 40 mats but only 12 baskets, which is 22 - 12 = 10 baskets short at an unchanged output of mats. So March sits inside the boundary: some of the 12 members' time was idle or misused. The co-operative could therefore have raised baskets toward 22 without giving up any mats - spare capacity, not a limit.

items.prompt: An economy has been producing well inside its boundary, with boats in harbour and graduates without posts. Its government opens a training and placement scheme that is likely to move idle workers into the two industries, because the scheme pays firms to hire and train. Analyse the consequences for the economy's position relative to its PPC and for consumers, workers and the government.
items.canonical_answer: The economy starts inside its PPC, with idle boats and graduates without posts, so output is below what its resources allow. The scheme pays firms to hire and train, so idle workers start producing and output of one or both goods rises with no sacrifice of the other. The economy therefore moves from its interior point toward the boundary; the curve itself does not shift. Consumers get more goods, workers earn wages instead of waiting, and the government collects more tax as activity rises. These gains depend on the posts matching the training, and once the economy reaches its boundary, more of one good costs some of the other.

Mechanism: the causal link must be written out, because this causes that, step by step.

items.prompt: An economics club in Swakopmund argues about a picture of an economy's PPC with three dots marked on it. Explain the features that distinguish where each dot sits - under the boundary, on it, or beyond it - and what each location shows.
items.canonical_answer: A point on the boundary shows resources fully and efficiently employed: a maximum, where more of one good costs some of the other. A point under it shows resources idle or misused: one or both goods could rise without sacrifice. A point beyond it shows output current resources and technology cannot reach until the boundary shifts outward. The distinguishing feature is the comparison with a reachable combination: below it is inside, equal to it is on, above every one is beyond.

items.prompt: Define a movement along a production possibility curve.
items.canonical_answer: A movement along a PPC is a reallocation of resources between the two goods while the economy stays on the same boundary: more of one good, less of the other. The amount of the good given up is the opportunity cost.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must give the precise meaning of the term, and each creditable element of it is worth one mark.

items.prompt: Portugal's planners consider shifting workers and presses from wine bottling into machine-tool works, with the country's capacity for both goods unchanged this year. Discuss how a production possibility curve shows the change: state the axes to label, the original curve, the movement along it in the correct direction, the point the economy is marked at when the move ends, and what the diagram shows in words.
items.canonical_answer: Label the vertical axis bottled wine, in million litres a year, and the horizontal axis machine tools, in units a year. Draw PPC1 bowed outward between the intercepts. Mark A on it at 35 million litres of wine with 12 000 machine tools. The change is a movement along the curve: slide down PPC1 toward the machine-tool axis to B, 20 million litres of wine with 18 000 machine tools, and label B as the new combination. In words: machine tools rose by 18 000 - 12 000 = 6 000 and wine fell by 35 - 20 = 15 million litres, so 15 million litres of wine is the opportunity cost of the extra tools. Because capacity is unchanged, the curve stays where it is: this is a movement along it, not a shift.
marking_guidance: Axes labelled: bottled wine in million litres on one axis, machine tools in units on the other.
Original curves drawn and labelled: the single boundary drawn bowed outward and labelled PPC1 before the move is marked.
The shift or movement, in the correct direction: a movement along the curve from A toward the machine-tool axis, on the same boundary throughout.
New point marked and labelled: the finishing combination B marked and named on PPC1.
What the diagram shows, in words: the reallocation from wine to machine tools, with the opportunity cost stated in million litres.
The link: the fixed boundary carries the reallocation, and the consequence is the wine given up for the tools gained.

items.prompt: A highland economy sits at X on its boundary with 35 tonnes of wool and 15 tonnes of coffee, and considers Y, also on the boundary, with 25 tonnes of wool and 27 tonnes of coffee. Explain what the data shows about the cost of moving from X to Y.
items.canonical_answer: The data show a movement along the boundary: more coffee means less wool. The move gains 27 - 15 = 12 tonnes of coffee and gives up 35 - 25 = 10 tonnes of wool, so 10 tonnes of wool is the opportunity cost. This is because the same pastures and workers cannot serve both; as the move continues, resources less suited to coffee are switched, so each further tonne of coffee costs more wool. However, from a point inside the boundary, coffee could rise without any wool given up.

items.prompt: Oshakati Textiles runs two lines from the same 40 machinists: school shirts and work dresses. Because the same 40 machinists run both lines, workers and machines moved from shirts to dresses. Therefore the factory could still return to A whenever it chose.

items.prompt: A country on its production possibility boundary chooses, over a decade, to slide from a wine-heavy combination toward machine tools, cutting wine output year by year. Analyse the consequences of that movement along the curve for consumers, for workers in the two industries, and for the economy's future capacity.
items.canonical_answer: The country moves along its boundary from a wine-heavy combination toward machine tools, shifting resources from vineyards into tool works. Wine output falls each year while tool output rises, and the opportunity cost grows, because the workers least suited to tool-making are moved last, so each further batch of tools costs more wine. Consumers have less wine now, vineyard workers lose posts or retrain, and tool workers gain jobs and wages. The cost lands on today's wine consumers and vineyard workers; the return lands on tool workers and future consumers, provided the machines are kept running, because more capital goods can shift the boundary outward in later years.

items.prompt: A teacher asks a class to state what changes and what stays fixed when an economy slides along its PPC. Explain the features of a movement along a production possibility curve.
items.canonical_answer: The economy moves from one point on the boundary to another on the same boundary, toward the axis of the good being expanded. One output rises while the other falls, because resources are shifted between them. The boundary stays fixed: maximum possible output is unchanged, which separates a movement from a shift. And the movement carries an opportunity cost - the amount of the other good given up - which tends to rise as the movement continues.
marking_guidance: Features: the elements required are named in the answer, and one mark is earned per feature developed with what it shows.

items.prompt: Two learners argue about a country that has just built new engineering workshops and trained 5 000 extra technicians. One says the economy "has moved along its PPC"; the other says it "has shifted its PPC". Explain the confusion between a movement along a PPC and a shift of a PPC, and state the test that tells them apart.
items.canonical_answer: The learners mix up a change in the combination chosen with a change in what the economy can produce. A movement along a PPC keeps the same boundary and swaps one good for the other; a shift moves the boundary itself, so maximum output rises or falls. To tell them apart, ask whether the maximum possible output has changed: unchanged means a movement, changed means a shift. New workshops and 5 000 extra technicians raise what the economy can produce, so this is an outward shift.
marking_guidance: The confusion: what learners mix up must be named - a change in the combination chosen mistaken for a change in capacity.
The boundary between the ideas: a movement along keeps the maximum unchanged; a shift moves the maximum itself.
The test: ask what happened to the maximum possible output of both goods together - unchanged means a movement along the curve, changed means a shift of it.

items.prompt: After a drought ruins grazing land, a region can produce less beef and less milk than before. Define a shift of a production possibility curve.
items.canonical_answer: A shift of a PPC is a movement of the whole boundary. An outward shift shows productive capacity growing, so more of at least one good can be produced; an inward shift, as after the drought, shows capacity shrinking.

items.prompt: Brazil opens technical colleges that raise the productivity of its engineers and machine operators within a decade, adding skills without adding farmland. Discuss how a production possibility curve shows what the colleges did to the country's productive capacity: name the axes, the original curve, the direction the curve moves, where the new curve sits relative to the old one, the point the economy can now be marked at, and what the diagram shows in words.
items.canonical_answer: Label the vertical axis soyabeans, in million tonnes a year, and the horizontal axis aircraft, in units a year. Draw PPC1 bowed outward from 100 million tonnes of soyabeans to 40 aircraft. The colleges cause a shift, not a movement along the curve: draw PPC2 outward, away from the origin and beyond PPC1 at every point, from 120 million tonnes of soyabeans to 52 aircraft - gains of 120 - 100 = 20 million tonnes and 52 - 40 = 12 aircraft at the two ends. Mark a new point on PPC2, such as 39 aircraft with 80 million tonnes of soyabeans, which PPC1 could not reach. In words: more productive workers raised the country's capacity, so the whole boundary moved outward and combinations once beyond reach are now attainable.
marking_guidance: Axes labelled: soyabeans in million tonnes on one axis, aircraft in units per year on the other.
Original curves drawn and labelled: the first boundary drawn bowed outward and labelled PPC1 before the shift is drawn.
The shift or movement, in the correct direction: the whole curve shifts outward, away from the origin, to PPC2 - no slide along PPC1 is drawn.
New point marked and labelled: a combination on PPC2, beyond the old boundary, marked and named.
What the diagram shows, in words: capacity growth through skills, with once-unreachable combinations now reachable.
The link: skills raised what workers produce, and the consequence is the boundary relocating outward rather than a point moving along it.

items.prompt: A country's maximum outputs were measured in 2019 and again in 2026. In 2019 its production boundary reached 8 000 buses a year or 200 000 tonnes of wheat a year at the two ends; in 2026 the same measurement found 9 600 buses a year or 200 000 tonnes of wheat a year. Explain what the data shows about what happened to the country's productive capacity.
items.canonical_answer: The data show the boundary shifted outward at the bus end only. The bus maximum rose from 8 000 to 9 600 a year, an increase of 9 600 - 8 000 = 1 600 buses, while the wheat maximum stayed at 200 000 tonnes. This is because the country gained bus-building capacity - workshops, trained fitters - but no extra farmland, so the boundary pivoted outward around the wheat end. However, the data show capacity, not actual output: the country could still be producing inside its larger boundary.
marking_guidance: What the data shows: the relationship between the two outputs must be stated before anything else.
Supporting evidence: a comparison of two rows or steps in the data, with their figures.
Exception: an answer that notes where the reading does not go further (boundary maximums, unrecorded output, a point inside rather than on the curve) earns the however mark.
Why: the explanation of the relationship - scarce resources shared between the two goods, with the resources best suited to the expanding good moved first and the least suited last.

items.prompt: A Katutura printing co-operative sent its 9 members on a weekend course in press maintenance. Before the course its boundary ran to 4 500 posters a day or 1 800 banners a day; after the course the same members and presses can reach 5 400 posters a day or 2 160 banners a day. Using the figures, explain what happened to the co-operative's boundary and what that change shows.
items.canonical_answer: Before the course the maximums were 4 500 posters or 1 800 banners a day; after it, 5 400 posters or 2 160 banners. That is 5 400 - 4 500 = 900 more posters and 2 160 - 1 800 = 360 more banners from the same 9 members and presses, so the whole boundary shifted outward: capacity grew. The cause is higher productivity, not more members. Therefore a combination once out of reach, such as 4 800 posters with 600 banners, may now be attainable.
marking_guidance: Context: the figures in the prompt must be used - no answer without them.
Reasoning: the link from the figures to the concept must be written out, because figures stated without the link earn nothing.
Conclusion: therefore the answer ends by saying what the figures show about the boundary.

items.prompt: A flood destroys a third of the fishing boats and two processing halls of a lakeside economy. Analyse the consequences for the economy's production possibility boundary and for its consumers, its fish workers and its government budget.
items.canonical_answer: The flood destroys a third of the boats and two processing halls, so the economy's stock of capital falls. With fewer boats and halls, maximum fish output falls at every combination, so the boundary itself shifts inward: capacity has shrunk, not just the choice. Consumers face less fish, and fish workers lose crew and processing posts. The government faces rebuilding costs that are likely to crowd other spending, such as schools and roads, out of its budget. How fast the boundary recovers depends on how quickly the capital is replaced; meanwhile the economy can still use what remains to reach its smaller boundary.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change must be stated, as a when or an if.
Mechanism: the causal link must be written out, because this causes that, step by step.
Consequence: therefore the results are traced to output, employment or capacity.
For whom: each consequence is named for the consumer, the worker, the firm or the economy it lands on.

items.prompt: A news report says a country's "capacity to produce has grown for a fifth straight year". Explain the features of a shift of a production possibility curve that would show such growth.
items.canonical_answer: The whole boundary moves rather than a point sliding along it. An outward shift shows productive capacity growing, so more of at least one good can be produced; it tends to come from more resources, better-trained workers or better technology. An inward shift shows capacity shrinking, as when resources are destroyed. A point once beyond the old boundary may lie on or inside the new one: what the economy can reach has changed, not just the combination chosen.
marking_guidance: Features: the elements required are named in the answer, and one mark is earned per feature developed with what it shows.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. A production possibility curve shows:
A  the combinations of two goods an economy actually consumes
B  the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with resources fully employed
C  the prices of two goods over a year
D  the profits of the two largest firms

2. The PPC slopes downward from left to right because:
A  resources are scarce, so more of one good means less of the other
B  consumers prefer variety
C  prices fall as output rises
D  governments tax the second good

3. A point inside the boundary shows:
A  resources idle or misused
B  resources fully employed
C  an output beyond reach
D  a shift of the boundary

4. A point beyond the boundary shows:
A  full employment of resources
B  idle resources
C  an output the current resources and technology cannot reach
D  a fall in capacity

5. Moving from one point on the boundary to another point on the same boundary shows:
A  growth of capacity
B  a reallocation between the two goods, with an opportunity cost
C  idle resources coming into use
D  a fall in the maximum output

6. The opportunity cost of moving along the boundary toward good X is:
A  the money spent on good X
B  the amount of the other good given up
C  the change in the price of good X
D  the number of workers who move

7. An outward shift of the whole boundary shows:
A  the economy chose a different combination
B  growth of the economy's productive capacity
C  unemployment of resources
D  a movement along the boundary

8. Which is most likely to shift an economy's PPC outward?
A  a decision to produce more of one good and less of the other
B  a rise in unemployment
C  training that raises the skills of workers
D  a bad harvest
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 A, 3 A, 4 C, 5 B, 6 B, 7 B, 8 C.
1. B is the definition, a boundary of maximum combinations at full use; A confuses what is consumed with what can be produced, C confuses the boundary with a price record, D confuses an economy's curve with firm accounts.
2. A gives the mechanism, scarce resources shared between the goods; B, C and D each invent a cause that does not force the two outputs to trade off.
3. A: inside means idle or misused resources; B reads an interior point as a boundary point, C reverses inside and beyond, D mistakes a location for a change in the boundary.
4. C: beyond is unattainable at present; A and B swap the meanings of the three locations, D confuses an unattainable point with a fall in the boundary.
5. B: the same boundary, a new combination, a sacrifice; A mistakes a slide for a shift, C applies to a start inside the boundary, D reverses the direction of the change.
6. B: the cost is the other good given up, in its own units; A and C bring money and price into a curve measured in goods, D counts the means rather than the cost.
7. B: the whole curve moving outward is capacity growth; A and D read a shift as a slide, C confuses a location with a change in the boundary.
8. C: skills raise what resources can produce, moving the boundary; A is a movement along the boundary, B pushes the economy inside it, D is a fall in output, not in capacity.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark per question; the correct option for each question is listed and every distractor is explained as the specific misunderstanding it catches.

Distractors that merely restate the question catch nothing; each wrong option traces to a named error - a location read as a shift, a slide read as a shift, capacity read as choice, consumption read as production.

items.prompt:
A survey of the Kavango East regional economy, 2026. The region grows mahangu, a pearl millet, and farms tilapia in ponds. Engineers mapped what the region could reach in a normal season at full and efficient use: all resources in the fields gives 6 000 tonnes of mahangu with no tilapia; all in the ponds gives 1 000 tonnes of tilapia with no mahangu; a surveyed mixed combination reaches 3 600 tonnes of mahangu together with 600 tonnes of tilapia. Last season the region actually produced 3 600 tonnes of mahangu and 450 tonnes of tilapia, with pond gates standing idle. From March, a new irrigation scheme is expected to lift the mahangu maximum to 7 500 tonnes, with the tilapia maximum unchanged.

Table 1 - Kavango East, normal-season boundary and last season
  all fields: 6 000 tonnes of mahangu, no tilapia
  surveyed mix: 3 600 tonnes of mahangu, 600 tonnes of tilapia
  all ponds: no mahangu, 1 000 tonnes of tilapia
  actual last season: 3 600 tonnes of mahangu, 450 tonnes of tilapia
  after irrigation: 7 500 tonnes of mahangu maximum, 1 000 tonnes of tilapia maximum

(a) The surveyed mix and last season had the same mahangu output. Calculate the shortfall in tilapia output against the surveyed mix. [1]
(b) Calculate actual mahangu output as a share of the all-fields maximum. [1]
(c) Identify the two goods the region produces. [2]
(d) Explain what the figures show about how fully the region used its resources last season. [4]
(e) Analyse what the irrigation scheme is likely to change for the region's boundary and for its farmers and fish workers. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) 600 - 450 = 150 tonnes of tilapia.
(b) 3 600 / 6 000 = 0.60, which is 60% of the all-fields maximum.
(c) Mahangu, a pearl millet [1], and farmed tilapia [1].
(d) The figures show the region produced inside its boundary last season. At the surveyed mix, 3 600 tonnes of mahangu goes with 600 tonnes of tilapia; last season delivered the same 3 600 tonnes of mahangu with 450 tonnes of tilapia, short by 150 tonnes on one good at an unchanged other. An output below a reachable combination on one good, holding the other, places the season inside the boundary, so the pond resources behind the idle gates were not fully used. Because the region is inside, tilapia could rise toward 600 tonnes without any mahangu being given up, which is what producing inside a boundary shows: spare capacity rather than a limit.
(e) Expected relationship: the irrigation scheme raises the mahangu maximum, so the region's boundary shifts outward at the mahangu end - a shift of the curve, not a movement along it. Evidence from the data: the mahangu maximum rises from 6 000 to 7 500 tonnes, a gain of 1 500 tonnes, while the tilapia maximum stays at 1 000 tonnes, so the boundary pivots outward around the tilapia end. Analysis: with the boundary further out, combinations of mahangu and tilapia once beyond reach become reachable; farmers can grow more mahangu with the same effort, and the region's actual point can rise toward the new boundary. The consequence for farmers is more possible output and income; for fish workers the change in what is possible is small, though their own maximum of 1 000 tonnes was already under-used last season at 450 tonnes, so their room to grow lies inside the old boundary. Exception: where water rights, seed or labour limit planting, the extra maximum may not turn into extra output, and the shift says nothing about use - a region can sit inside a grown boundary exactly as before.
marking_guidance: Parts: (a) and (b) are 1 mark each and must be exact calculations from Table 1; (c) is 2 marks, 1 per good; (d) is 4 marks, one per distinct linked statement; (e) is 6 marks.

(e) must run the expected relationship, then evidence from the data, then analysis, then an exception; quoting a figure from Table 1 is evidence, not analysis - a figure without the linked statement it supports earns nothing in (e).
For whom: consequences in (e) are named for farmers, for fish workers and for the region.

facts: boundary mix 3 600 tonnes mahangu with 600 tonnes tilapia
after irrigation 7 500 tonnes mahangu maximum, 1 000 tonnes tilapia maximum

items.prompt:
An economy produces machinery and grain.
(a) Define its production possibility curve. [2]
(b) Explain what a point inside, a point on and a point beyond the curve each show. [4]
(c) Analyse the consequences for consumers and workers of the economy moving along its curve from a grain-heavy combination to a machinery-heavy combination. [6]
(d) Discuss whether the economy should choose a machinery-heavy point on its curve now. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) A production possibility curve is a boundary showing the maximum combinations of two goods - here machinery and grain - that the economy can produce in a given period when its resources are employed fully and efficiently.
(b) A point on the curve shows resources fully and efficiently employed, so output is at a maximum for that combination of machinery and grain. A point inside the curve shows resources idle or misused, so output of machinery or grain, or both, could be higher without sacrifice. A point beyond the curve shows an output the current resources and technology cannot produce; it becomes reachable if the boundary shifts outward through growth of capacity. Placing a point is a comparison against a reachable combination: below it on one or both goods is inside, equal to it is on, above every reachable combination is beyond.
(c) The economy sits on its boundary at a grain-heavy combination and moves along the boundary toward machinery. Because resources shift from farms to machine works, grain output falls and machinery rises; the opportunity cost of the machinery grows as the move continues, because the farmers least productive at grain give up little grain first, so each later machine costs more grain than the one before. Consumers face less grain now, so food costs rise or imports must fill the gap; farm workers lose posts or retrain for machine works, and machine workers gain posts and wages. The cost lands on today's consumers and farm workers, while the return lands on machine workers and on future consumers, provided the machinery is kept running - machines make machines, so the economy's future capacity tends to rise with the machine stock, which is a change to the boundary itself in the years after the move.
(d) Why it might: a machinery-heavy point builds the capital that makes later production easier, so the boundary tends to shift outward in the years that follow and consumers later enjoy more of both goods; machine workers gain skilled, better-paid posts, and the economy imports less machinery. Why it might not: the grain given up now is food, and consumers face higher food costs or shortages in the present; where grain cannot be imported, the cost lands on households directly, and the rising opportunity cost means each extra machine costs more grain than the last. Judgement: on balance the machinery-heavy point is worth choosing where the population can be fed meanwhile - through imports, stocks or rising farm productivity - and that is the condition the judgement depends on. Where food security is fragile, the grain-heavy point comes first, and the move toward machinery waits a season.
marking_guidance: Parts: (a) 2 marks for two creditable elements of the definition; (b) 4 marks, one per distinct linked statement; (c) 6 marks, one per distinct linked statement with its reason carried; (d) 8 marks, level-marked over three bands.

Bands for (d): Level 3 (top) examines why it might and why it might not, then reaches a judgement naming the condition it depends on; Level 2 develops one side or asserts a judgement without the condition; Level 1 offers fragments of either side.
For whom: (c) must name the consumer and the worker at each step, and (d) must land its costs and returns on named parties.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "A coastal economy spends heavily on new fishing academies and boatyards. Discuss whether this shifts the economy production possibility curve outward." Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for (the boundary shifts outward):
Point 1: boatyards add capital and academies add skills, and both raise what the economy can produce, which is what an outward shift means. Chain: academies open, crews trained, more fish caught per boat per season, the fish maximum rises, the boundary moves outward (for fishers, for consumers).
Point 2: the skills transfer beyond the fleet. Chain: navigators and engineers trained for the sea take some posts in harbours and repairs, harbour output rises, the other end of the boundary rises a little too (for workers, for firms).
Case against (the boundary may not shift):
Point 1: resources spent on academies and yards are taken from today's fishing, so the economy first slides along its current boundary - a cost now, not a capacity gain. Chain: yards built, workers and materials diverted, present fish output falls, the economy sits at a point further along the same curve (for today's consumers and fishers).
Point 2: the new capacity lasts where it is kept. Chain: trained crews leave for other coasts, boats decay without maintenance, the maximum falls back, the boundary drifts inward (for the economy, for consumers).
Judgement: the academies and boatyards are likely to shift the boundary outward over time, and the condition the judgement depends on is whether the trained crews stay and the fleet is kept seaworthy; without that condition the spending buys a slide along the old curve and a decayed fleet, and the boundary ends where it began.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the case for, the case against, each point as a chain, and the judgement with the condition it depends on.
Each chain states its starting point, its mechanism and the consequence for a named party - consumer, worker, firm or economy.
The judgement must settle on the condition: what would have to hold for the shift to be real and lasting.
